title: Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane)

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: An abstract painting of flat geometric shapes in several colors, arranged across a light background so that they seem to move and fly.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement); collection not stated on the page

context: An oil painting on canvas by the Russian artist Olga Rozanova, dated 1916 on its source page, which tags it Abstract Art and Geometric Art. Its title refers to the flight of an airplane without showing a recognizable plane.

descriptions.k: Look at all the shapes and colors. They do not show a real thing. The title says airplane. Can you feel something flying?
descriptions.g12: Olga Rozanova made this painting from flat shapes and bright colors. There are no people or objects. The title says Flight of an Airplane. How do the shapes seem to zoom or float?
descriptions.g35: Olga Rozanova painted Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane) in 1916. Non-objective means it does not show real objects, only shapes and colors. The title gives a clue about flight. How do the shapes and their direction suggest movement through the air?
descriptions.g68: Rozanova's Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane, 1916) belongs to Suprematism, a Russian movement that used pure geometric forms and color. The title suggests a theme of flight, but no plane appears. How do tilted shapes, overlaps and color contrasts create a feeling of movement and height?
descriptions.g910: Olga Rozanova's Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane, 1916) shows how Suprematist artists replaced depiction with relationships among planes of color. Flight, a new experience in the early twentieth century, appears only through the title and the painting's dynamics. How do the shapes build speed, balance and space, and what does abstraction allow that a picture of a plane cannot?
descriptions.g1112: Rozanova's Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane, 1916) places her within the Russian avant-garde and Suprematism, where geometric forms were meant to express a new way of seeing. A woman artist in a movement often told through men, she links the abstract surface to the modern experience of flight. How might the work be read as perception, as celebration of technology, or as an argument for abstraction?

k.daily: Look at the shapes. Which one looks like it is flying fastest?
k.emotion: How do these bright shapes make you feel, calm or excited?
k.observation: Find a triangle or a rectangle. Where is it?
k.analysis: Which shapes are big, and which are small?
k.line: Trace a slanted line with your finger. Where does it point?
k.shape: Find a shape that touches another shape. What do they look like together?
k.color: Which colors in Flight of an Airplane are your favorites?
k.texture: The shapes look smooth and flat. How might the painting feel if you touched it?
k.space: Which shapes feel high up, and which feel low down?
k.light: Where do you see the lightest color in the painting?
k.meaning: The title says airplane, but there is no plane. What do you imagine?
k.culture: This painting is from Russia. What would you tell a friend about it?
k.technique: The painter used flat shapes instead of drawing a plane. How is that different?
k.personal: If you could make your own flying picture with shapes, what shapes would you use?
k.critical: What would you move or change in Rozanova's painting to make it zoom more?

g12.daily: How do the shapes in Flight of an Airplane make you imagine something moving through the sky?
g12.emotion: What mood do the bright flat colors give you, and which shapes make you feel it?
g12.observation: List the shapes and colors you see, then say which ones seem to move.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to certain shapes before others?
g12.line: How do slanted lines in the painting give a feeling of speed?
g12.shape: How do the shapes overlap or touch to make a bigger design?
g12.color: How do different colors help the shapes stand out from the light background?
g12.texture: This painting looks smooth and flat. How does that change the way it feels to look at?
g12.space: How does the painting make some shapes feel closer and others farther away?
g12.light: Where do you see lighter and darker colors, and what do they do?
g12.meaning: Why might a painter show flight with shapes instead of drawing an airplane?
g12.culture: What can this painting from Russia in 1916 tell us about artists who tried new ideas?
g12.technique: How can an artist use only shapes and color to make a picture?
g12.personal: How would you draw the feeling of flying without drawing a plane?
g12.critical: Why do you think some people enjoy paintings with no real objects?

g35.daily: Which parts of Non-Objective Composition (Flight of an Airplane) give you a feeling of movement?
g35.emotion: What feeling do the colors and shapes give you, and what supports it?
g35.observation: Study the shapes. Which repeat, and where does the pattern change?
g35.analysis: How does the way the shapes are arranged guide your eyes across the painting?
g35.line: How do diagonal and straight lines change the speed and direction of your eye?
g35.shape: How do the sizes of the shapes create a main shape and smaller helpers?
g35.color: How do contrasting colors help separate one shape from another?
g35.texture: The surface looks flat and smooth. What does that tell you about how the shapes were painted?
g35.space: How does the painting suggest depth, or refuse to, using only flat shapes?
g35.light: How does the contrast of lighter and darker colors affect how the shapes seem to float?
g35.meaning: Why might Rozanova have named the painting after flight without painting an airplane?
g35.culture: What does this painting tell us about Russian artists in 1916 who wanted to leave behind pictures of real objects?
g35.technique: How is painting flat color shapes different from blending soft colors?
g35.personal: What would you want to ask Olga Rozanova about turning flight into shapes?
g35.critical: Some viewers say abstract paintings are easy to make. What evidence from this painting suggests careful decisions?

g68.daily: How does Rozanova use shape and direction to suggest flight without painting an airplane?
g68.emotion: Which choices of color and arrangement give the painting energy and lift?
g68.observation: Compare how crowded and open areas are handled. What differences stand out?
g68.analysis: How does the composition use tilted shapes to guide your eye and suggest movement?
g68.line: How do diagonal edges differ in effect from horizontal and vertical ones?
g68.shape: How do the geometric shapes work together as a system rather than as separate objects?
g68.color: How does the contrast of vivid and subdued colors create rhythm across the surface?
g68.texture: How does the flat application of paint support the idea of pure shape?
g68.space: How do overlapping and spacing of shapes imitate depth, and where does the painting remain flat?
g68.light: How do lighter and darker colors stand in for the light and shade you would see in a realistic scene?
g68.meaning: What might Rozanova be saying about modern flight by choosing non-objective forms?
g68.culture: How might the excitement about flight and new technology in the early twentieth century shape this painting?
g68.technique: What does non-objective mean, and how does it affect the techniques the painter needs?
g68.personal: What emotions would you read in the painting, and what would you avoid claiming without more evidence?
g68.critical: Does a painting need to show recognizable things to communicate an idea? Use details from this painting to explain.

g910.daily: Which formal decisions in Flight of an Airplane let abstract planes carry the sensation of movement and height?
g910.emotion: What emotional or energetic tone results from the arrangement and color contrasts, and how is it built?
g910.observation: Examine how shapes meet and overlap. What do the junctions suggest about the painter's priorities?
g910.analysis: How does the placement of larger and smaller planes establish a hierarchy within a non-objective composition?
g910.line: How do diagonals and tilts establish dynamism, and how do any stabilizing lines counter them?
g910.shape: How do the simplified geometric shapes operate as a visual vocabulary rather than as a depiction?
g910.color: How does the interplay of saturated and neutral colors structure the field?
g910.texture: How does the flat paint handling reinforce the surface as a plane of color?
g910.space: How does overlapping substitute for traditional perspective, and how does it still imply space?
g910.light: How does value contrast help the shapes advance or recede without naturalistic modeling?
g910.meaning: How might the title, naming flight, guide interpretation of an otherwise non-objective work?
g910.culture: How does the painting reflect the Russian avant-garde's belief in a new visual language around 1916?
g910.technique: How does Suprematist technique differ from academic painting in what it asks the painter to control?
g910.personal: What does the painting make you consider about experiences that are hard to depict directly, like flight?
g910.critical: To what extent does abstraction strengthen the idea of flight, and where might a representational image do more?

g1112.daily: How does the tension between a title that names flight and a surface that shows no plane allow Non-Objective Composition to support competing readings?
g1112.emotion: Might the sense of speed belong to the painting or to the expectations the title creates? Weigh the visual evidence.
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions of overlapping planes. How do these thresholds shape your sense of space and motion?
g1112.analysis: How does the asymmetrical balance of shapes produce a dynamic equilibrium instead of a single focal point?
g1112.line: How does the use of diagonal tilt relate to Suprematist ideas of a new, weightless space?
g1112.shape: In what ways do the geometric forms operate as pure elements, and in what ways do they still evoke the world?
g1112.color: How does the color system serve a conception of rhythm and contrast rather than description?
g1112.texture: How does the flatness of the surface connect to ideas about the painting as an autonomous object?
g1112.space: How does the ambiguous space respond to the early twentieth-century change in how people imagined height and distance after flight?
g1112.light: How does value contrast operate where traditional light and shadow are absent?
g1112.meaning: How does the work position Rozanova within, and potentially beyond, narratives of Suprematism that often center other artists?
g1112.culture: How do the conditions of Russia in 1916, as widely known, complicate any simple reading of abstraction as escape from the world?
g1112.technique: How does non-objective painting challenge assumptions about skill, representation and what counts as a subject?
g1112.personal: How does your own expectation that art should show something recognizable shape your response, and does this painting meet or resist it?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that the title limits rather than opens the painting, and how would you answer it?

teacherNote.context: A 1916 oil painting by the Russian artist Olga Rozanova, tagged on its source page as Abstract Art and Geometric Art; the page does not state the collection. The title refers to flight, but the painting shows no recognizable airplane.
directions: Have students cut colored paper shapes and arrange them to suggest flight, then compare arrangements.
Ask students to give the painting a different title and discuss how the new title changes what they see.
Discuss how an artist can show an experience, such as flying, without showing its usual objects.
